segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "there is" or "there are"—"there is" or "there are"—in most languages, this is a separate verb,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but in English, we are expressing it with the combination of "there" and "is" or "are". In Spanish, to say "there is" or "there are",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: we have hay. H-a-y. And hay is actually from haber.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hay.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hay. And for once, we have a situation where it's changing in English and it's not changing in Spanish. Hay means "there is" or "there are", it's not changing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "somebody" is alguien. Alguien.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Alguien.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say "There is somebody here that wants to speak with you", and let's speak formally: "There is somebody here that wants to speak with you"? So the first bit is "There is somebody here".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hay alguien aquí...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "...that wants to speak with you", speaking formally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...que quiere hablar con usted.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Hay alguien aquí que quiere hablar con usted. "There is somebody here that wants to speak with you."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if you say "Is there somebody here that speaks Spanish?", and you specify with your subjectivity—this thing that we don't know if it exists or not, this somebody that speaks Spanish—

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and you do that with this que structure: "Is there somebody here that speaks Spanish?", and here you will use the mood tense, this subjective tense. So how would you say that: "Is there somebody here that speaks Spanish?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Hay alguien aquí que hable español?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. ¿Hay alguien aquí que hable español?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if somebody replies to you: "There are two people that speak Spanish here. There are two people here that speak Spanish." Do you think you will use the mood tense?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No, they're just saying what there is. So "There are two people"—which in Spanish is "There are two persons"—so "There are two people here"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hay dos personas aquí...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...that speak Spanish.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...que hablan español.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Hay dos personas aquí que hablan español. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The past of hay is había, which shows us actually that hay comes from haber. It's a very weird historic version of haber, but había we see more clearly that it comes from haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now había doesn't change either, so you will have to resist the temptation to say habían when you want to say "there were" instead of "there was". No, it's always había. Doesn't change. Hay doesn't change for "there is" or "there are" and había doesn't change for "there was" or "there were".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "There were two people that spoke Spanish"? Now this is an interesting sentence because in English, we will use the point in the past: "There were two people that spoke Spanish".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But what do you think we will use in Spanish: the point or the line?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: The line.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Because I've heard Spaniards speaking in English saying it that way.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ah, yeah! So you've really heard the negative language transfer. Oh, that's great! So it makes sense for it to be the line in the past because what we're referring to here is the fact they were Spanish speakers,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and they weren't Spanish speakers just for that moment, were they? So if we look at it and we think about which one fits better, we will choose the line.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So again, it's a great example that we don't want to take a direct translation from English from "spoke"; we want to just look at the context and decide if it makes sense to use the line or the point. So give me this sentence:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "There were two people here that spoke Spanish."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Había dos personas aquí que hablaban español.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Había dos personas aquí que hablaban español. If we were to use the point here, que hablaron español, we wouldn't be talking about the fact that they are Spanish speakers, but rather that they spoke Spanish at that time, whatever time we're referring to.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that hay, "there is" or "there are", or había, "there was" or "there were", comes from haber, in fact.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So when we say something like "there has to be something", and with this "be", we mean "exist"—"there has to exist something"—this "be" is actually coming from "there is/there are", not from "to be".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's coming from this invisible verb that we do not have in English, which we make up for by using "there is/there are".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So when we say something like "There has to be something that you can eat", "There must be something that you can do", this "be" is "exist"—"there must exist something". In which case, it's haber. It's not ser and it's not estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And if you try to think which one it is, ser or estar, you will be a long time trying to work out which one it is. So how would you say this sentence: "There has to be something that you can do."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Let's speak informally: "There has to be something that you can do." You can use "has to" or "must", doesn't make a lot of difference here.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tiene que hay...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That is "to" form, uh? So hay and había come from...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Haber.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tiene que haber...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...something that you can do.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...algo que puedas hacer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes! Puedas, very good. Tiene que haber algo que puedas hacer. Because here, like before with the example of "Is there somebody that speaks Spanish?", we are speaking about the existence of something when we don't know whether it exists or not, with this structure of hay and que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we're seeing that the mood tense has structural limitations: it can occur only in certain places structurally, and at the same time, only to give certain meanings or feelings.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now these meanings or feelings and the fact that Spanish is concerned with us expressing them and perceiving them through the language shows the value system of Spanish or part of the value system of Spanish. Now, different languages have different value systems: what...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: what a language requires you to express through it, and then the other things that the language might ignore, might be considered its value system. And languages, like cultures and individuals, have things they value, things they pay attention to, and things they don't.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which is what makes something like the mood tense so incredibly interesting to analyze and observe and use. So again, not something we want to be obsessed about getting correct; it really is something that we want to feel and also understand logically through our exposure and use of Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We should also bear in mind that the use of the subjunctive or the mood tense can change slightly depending on dialect and also idiolect, which is the individual dialect of each person.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we want to look out for it, listen actively, analyze, and enjoy the journey of understanding it and also using it and the different possibilities of expression that that gives us. It will be a very fascinating insight into the value system of this particular language.
